unit.name: Biology: Keeping Healthy
unit.subtitle: Pathogens, immunity, and how lifestyle choices shape disease risk.

lessons.title: Pathogens and Disease
lessons.description: How bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists cause communicable disease in humans and plants.
lessons.content_html:
Health and Disease

Health is a state of physical and mental well-being — not simply the absence of illness. Disease disrupts the normal functioning of cells and tissues, producing symptoms. Diseases fall into two broad categories: communicable diseases, which can be passed between organisms, and non-communicable diseases, which cannot. Understanding the causes and routes of spread of communicable diseases is essential for preventing and controlling them in both human and plant populations.

Key Fact

Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens — microorganisms that infect a host and cause harm. The four main types of pathogen are bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists. Each causes disease differently and requires a different approach to treatment or prevention.

The Four Types of Pathogen

Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes. They can reproduce rapidly inside the body and cause disease in two main ways: by producing toxins (poisonous substances that damage host tissues) or by directly invading and destroying cells. Examples of human bacterial diseases include Salmonella food poisoning (transmitted through contaminated food or water) and Gonorrhoea (a bacterial sexually transmitted infection). Crown gall disease, caused by the bacterium Agrobacterium tumefaciens, affects plants by producing tumour-like growths on stems and roots.

Viruses are not cells — they are much smaller than bacteria and cannot reproduce outside a living host cell. Once inside, a virus injects its genetic material and hijacks the cell’s machinery to make thousands of new virus particles. The cell is often destroyed as new viruses burst out. Human viral diseases include influenza (spread by airborne droplets), HIV (spread through bodily fluids, causing AIDS), and in plants, tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) which causes distinctive mosaic patterning on leaves and reduces photosynthesis.

Fungi cause disease by growing on host tissue and releasing enzymes that break down cells. Athlete’s foot is a common human fungal infection affecting the skin between the toes. Ash dieback is a serious fungal disease that has devastated ash tree populations across Europe; the fungus prevents water flow through the tree, causing progressive dieback of branches and often death of the tree.

Protists are single-celled eukaryotes. The malaria parasite (Plasmodium) is a protist transmitted by the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. Once inside the human body, the parasite infects and destroys red blood cells, causing the cycles of fever that characterise malaria. Mosquitoes act as vectors — they carry the parasite between human hosts without being harmed by it themselves.

How Pathogens Spread

Different pathogens use different routes to move between hosts. Understanding transmission routes is central to designing effective prevention strategies. Common routes include:

  • Airborne droplets: coughing or sneezing releases tiny droplets carrying pathogens. Influenza spreads this way.
  • Direct contact: touching an infected person or surface. Athlete’s foot spreads through contact with contaminated surfaces in warm, damp places.
  • Contaminated food or water: Salmonella is ingested in undercooked food or water contaminated with infected animal waste.
  • Bodily fluids: HIV is transmitted through blood, sexual contact, and from mother to child during birth or breastfeeding.
  • Animal vectors: malaria is transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes; the mosquito carries the parasite but does not develop the disease itself.
Key Fact

Plant diseases in this topic: tobacco mosaic virus (viral) — mosaic leaf patterns, reduced photosynthesis; ash dieback (fungal) — branch dieback and tree death; crown gall disease (bacterial) — tumour-like growths on stems and roots. All three can devastate populations of their host plant species.

The Body’s Natural Barriers

The human body has several non-specific defences that prevent pathogens from entering in the first place. These are described as non-specific because they act against any pathogen — they do not require the body to have encountered the pathogen before. The skin forms a physical barrier — unbroken skin is impermeable to most pathogens. In the respiratory tract, mucus traps pathogens and tiny hair-like structures called cilia sweep the mucus (with its trapped pathogens) away from the lungs. The stomach produces acid at a very low pH that kills most ingested pathogens. Tears and saliva contain enzymes (lysozyme) that break down bacterial cell walls. Beneficial bacteria in the gut occupy the available space and resources, competing with pathogens and making it harder for them to establish an infection.

If a pathogen does breach these first-line defences and enters the bloodstream or tissues, the immune system responds specifically to that pathogen. White blood cells called lymphocytes produce antibodies that bind to antigens on the pathogen’s surface, disabling or marking it for destruction. Other white blood cells can engulf and digest pathogens directly — a process called phagocytosis. Understanding these defences is essential for understanding how vaccines and other interventions work to enhance the body’s natural protection.

Plants have physical defences including a waxy leaf cuticle that prevents pathogen entry, and a cellulose cell wall that pathogens must breach to infect the cell. Plants also have chemical defences: they can produce antimicrobial substances in response to infection that slow or prevent pathogen spread within plant tissues. These active responses mean that the plant’s immune system, though simpler than a mammal’s, is dynamic — it responds to infection rather than simply acting as a passive barrier.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about specific diseases, always state the type of pathogen (virus, bacterium, fungus or protist) and the route of transmission — two separate points that each earn marks. For plant diseases specifically, you are expected to recall tobacco mosaic virus, ash dieback and crown gall disease by name. If asked to ‘explain’ how a pathogen causes disease (not just ‘state’), include the mechanism: toxin production for bacteria, cell destruction for viruses, enzyme release for fungi, or cell invasion for protists.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens: bacteria (produce toxins or invade cells), viruses (hijack host cell machinery), fungi (release enzymes), and protists (invade and destroy cells). Each group has distinct examples in humans and plants.
  • Key named diseases: influenza and HIV (viral), Salmonella and crown gall (bacterial), Athlete’s foot and ash dieback (fungal), malaria (protist via mosquito vector), tobacco mosaic virus (viral, plant).
  • Pathogens spread via airborne droplets, direct contact, contaminated food/water, bodily fluids and animal vectors. The body’s non-specific defences (skin, mucus, stomach acid, lysozymes, gut bacteria) act as a first line of defence against all pathogens.

practice_questions.text: Name the type of pathogen that causes each of the following diseases: (a) influenza  (b) malaria  (c) athlete's foot  (d) tobacco mosaic virus in plants.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: all four correct — (a) virus, (b) protist, (c) fungus, (d) virus. Two marks for four correct. Secure: three correct. Developing: two correct. Emerging: one correct.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the malaria parasite is transmitted from one human host to another.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: the malaria parasite (Plasmodium, a protist) is carried by female Anopheles mosquitoes; the mosquito bites an infected person and takes up the parasite; the mosquito later bites another person, transferring the parasite into their bloodstream; the parasite infects red blood cells. Secure: mosquito as vector identified; transmission mechanism described; one step vague. Developing: states mosquito bites transmit malaria without identifying the parasite type or process. Emerging: vague reference to insects spreading disease.

practice_questions.text: Explain why viruses are more difficult to treat than bacterial infections.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: viruses reproduce inside host cells using the cell's own machinery; antibiotics target structures specific to bacteria (e.g. cell wall) but cannot kill viruses without damaging host cells; antiviral drugs exist but are harder to design because of this; the body's immune system must largely fight off viral infections. Secure: states viruses are inside cells and antibiotics don't work on viruses; mechanism of why partially explained. Developing: states antibiotics don't work on viruses but does not explain why. Emerging: states viruses are hard to treat without scientific reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Describe three non-specific defences that protect the human body against pathogens.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: any three from — skin (impermeable physical barrier); mucus and cilia in airways (traps and sweeps pathogens away from lungs); stomach acid (low pH kills ingested pathogens); tears/saliva lysozyme (enzyme breaks down bacterial cell walls); gut bacteria (compete with pathogens). Each defence described with its mechanism. Three defences with mechanisms = four marks. Secure: three defences named but one or two mechanisms missing. Developing: two defences with mechanisms. Emerging: one or two defences named without mechanisms.

practice_questions.text: A plant disease is spreading rapidly through a local woodland, causing trees to show leaf discolouration and reduced growth. A scientist suspects a fungal pathogen. Describe how the scientist could identify whether the pathogen is fungal, and explain one method to prevent further spread.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: describes taking a sample from an infected plant; culturing on agar; microscopy to identify fungal structures (hyphae, spores); or DNA analysis to confirm identity; notes that correct identification is essential before choosing a control strategy; prevention method: removing and destroying infected trees, preventing movement of infected material, chemical fungicide treatment, or biological control — with mechanism explained and reliability considered. Secure: identification method described adequately; prevention method with partial reasoning. Developing: mentions culture or microscopy but method is vague; prevention stated without explanation. Emerging: general reference to 'testing' without scientific method.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a communicable and a non-communicable disease, with one example of each.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: communicable = caused by a pathogen, can spread between organisms (e.g. influenza/Salmonella/HIV); non-communicable = not caused by an infection, cannot be passed on (e.g. type 2 diabetes/cancer/cardiovascular disease). Both defined with examples. Secure: both types defined correctly; one example missing. Developing: one type defined correctly. Emerging: vague distinction without reference to pathogens or examples.

glossary_terms.definition: Diseases caused by pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi or protists) that can be transmitted from one organism to another.
Single-celled prokaryotic microorganisms. Pathogenic bacteria cause disease by producing toxins or by directly damaging host cells.
Non-cellular pathogens that can only reproduce inside a living host cell. Viruses take over the cell's machinery to produce copies of themselves, often destroying the cell in the process.
A viral plant disease caused by tobacco mosaic virus that causes a mosaic of light and dark patches on leaves, reducing photosynthesis and stunting growth.
A fungal disease of ash trees caused by the fungus Hymenoscyphus fraxineus. It causes leaf wilting, bark lesions and progressive death of branches.
Eukaryotic organisms that include moulds and yeasts. Pathogenic fungi cause disease by growing on or inside a host and releasing enzymes that damage tissue.
Single-celled eukaryotic microorganisms that are neither plants, animals, nor fungi. Some protists are pathogenic parasites.
Molecules (usually proteins) on the surface of a pathogen that are recognised as foreign by the immune system and trigger an immune response.
A waxy, waterproof layer on the outer surface of a leaf that acts as a physical barrier against pathogens.

lessons.title: Stopping Infection — Vaccination and Hygiene
lessons.description: How vaccines build immunity, why herd immunity matters, and how labs identify pathogens.
lessons.content_html:
Strategies to Prevent Infection

Preventing communicable diseases requires strategies that target the pathogen, the host, or the route of transmission. For plant diseases, strategies include sourcing disease-free plant material, rotating crops so pathogens cannot persist in one site, destroying infected plants to prevent spread, and using chemical or biological controls. For human diseases, strategies include vaccination, hygiene measures, sterilising wounds, contraception (for sexually transmitted infections), and restricting movement of infected individuals or animals. Each strategy has costs, benefits and risks that must be weighed, and an individual’s right to choose must be balanced against what is best for the wider population.

Key Fact

Prevention strategies for communicable diseases vary by context. For humans: vaccination, hygiene and sanitation, sterilisation of wounds, contraception (for STIs), and travel restrictions. For plants: using healthy seeds, crop rotation, polyculture, destroying infected plants, and chemical or biological pesticide use.

How Vaccination Works

A vaccine introduces a safe form of a pathogen — or parts of it — into the body. The immune system responds by producing white blood cells called lymphocytes, which make antibodies specific to the pathogen’s antigens (surface markers). Some of these lymphocytes persist in the body as memory cells.

If the real pathogen is encountered in future, the memory cells recognise its antigens immediately and mount a rapid secondary response — producing the correct antibodies much faster than a first-time immune response could. This speed means the infection is usually cleared before symptoms develop. This is immunity.

First exposure (or vaccination): the immune system takes several days to identify the antigen, activate the correct lymphocyte clone, and produce antibodies in significant quantities. During this time, the pathogen may replicate and symptoms can develop. However, memory cells are formed.

Second exposure: memory cells recognise the antigen almost immediately. Antibodies are produced rapidly, typically before any symptoms appear. The infection is controlled quickly. This is the secondary immune response — faster and stronger than the primary response, which is why vaccination with a safe form of the pathogen can protect against future infection with the real pathogen.

Herd Immunity

When a large proportion of a population is immune to a pathogen — either through vaccination or previous infection — the spread of the pathogen slows dramatically. This is called herd immunity. Immune individuals cannot pass the pathogen on, so the chain of transmission breaks before the pathogen reaches those who are not immune — including vulnerable people (such as newborns or immunocompromised individuals) who cannot receive certain vaccines.

Vaccination decisions involve weighing individual risk against collective benefit. A vaccine may carry a small risk of side effects; a person might question whether that risk is worth taking if most others around them are vaccinated and herd immunity already provides protection. However, if too many people reason this way, the proportion of immune individuals falls below the threshold needed for herd immunity, and outbreaks can follow. This is a classic tension in public health between individual rights and collective responsibility.

The likely effectiveness, benefits, risks and cost of vaccination programmes must be assessed by scientists and public health bodies. Where evidence shows benefits substantially outweigh risks across the population, vaccination is recommended. Where uptake is low, disease resurges — as has occurred with measles in some regions following misinformation about vaccine safety. Sound decisions in this area require understanding of data, scientific evidence, and how to evaluate competing claims.

Key Fact

Herd immunity works by breaking chains of transmission. When enough of the population is immune, a pathogen cannot find new hosts easily enough to spread. Vulnerable individuals (the very young, elderly, or immunocompromised) are protected indirectly because the pathogen rarely reaches them. The proportion of the population that must be immune varies by pathogen — it is generally higher for very infectious pathogens.

Identifying Pathogens in the Lab: Monoclonal Antibodies

Identifying which pathogen is causing an infection is essential for choosing the right treatment. Traditional methods include culturing samples on nutrient agar, observing colonies under a microscope, and testing sensitivity to antimicrobials. A more modern and highly specific method uses monoclonal antibodies.

First, an antigen (the target molecule) is injected into an animal, stimulating the immune system to produce antibody-producing lymphocytes. Cells producing the correct antibody are then identified and isolated. These cells are cultured to produce large quantities of identical antibodies, all of which recognise the same specific antigen. Because they come from a single clone of cells, they are called monoclonal (‘one clone’) antibodies.

Monoclonal antibodies can be used in diagnostic tests: if the target antigen is present in a sample (such as blood or urine), the antibody binds to it, producing a detectable signal. This approach is used in pregnancy tests (detecting a hormone produced in early pregnancy), in rapid diagnostic tests for certain infections, and in more sophisticated ELISA tests (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays) used in laboratories to identify pathogens or measure concentrations of substances in blood.

The high specificity of monoclonal antibodies — each antibody binds only to its precise target antigen — means diagnostic tests using them are more accurate and can produce results faster than traditional culture methods. This matters when rapid diagnosis allows quicker treatment decisions and reduces the spread of infections while a patient waits for results. New technologies based on monoclonal antibodies continue to be developed, with the potential to improve diagnosis of a wide range of conditions.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For vaccination questions, make sure you can describe both what a vaccine contains (a safe form of the pathogen) and how it confers immunity (stimulating antibody production and forming memory cells). Do not confuse the primary immune response (slow, first time) with the secondary immune response (fast, due to memory cells). For monoclonal antibody production, you must be able to describe the steps in sequence: antigen injected into animal → antibody-producing cells taken and selected → cells cultured to produce identical antibodies. On evaluate questions about vaccination, always weigh individual risk against collective (herd immunity) benefit — do not just list one side.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Vaccines contain a safe form of a pathogen. They stimulate the immune system to produce antibodies and memory cells without causing disease. When the real pathogen is encountered later, memory cells enable a rapid secondary response, preventing illness.
  • Herd immunity protects vulnerable individuals who cannot be vaccinated. If enough of the population is immune, chains of transmission break and outbreaks are prevented. Individual decisions about vaccination affect collective protection.
  • Monoclonal antibodies are produced by culturing cloned immune cells; all antibodies produced are identical and specific to one antigen. They are used in highly specific diagnostic tests (including ELISA) to identify pathogens rapidly and accurately.

Secure: three of four points present and linked. Developing: two points present; mechanism partially explained. Emerging: states vaccine prevents disease without explaining the immunological mechanism.

practice_questions.text: A new rapid diagnostic test uses monoclonal antibodies to detect a bacterial antigen in a blood sample. Evaluate the advantages of this approach compared with traditional bacterial culture.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: monoclonal antibodies are highly specific (only bind to the target antigen, reducing false positives); rapid result time compared to days needed for culture; can be used in a clinical setting without specialist microbiology lab; limitation: may only detect one specific pathogen so a negative result does not rule out other infections; traditional culture allows antibiotic sensitivity testing which the antibody test does not; overall evaluation — antibody test faster and highly specific but culture provides more information. Secure: advantages and at least one limitation clearly compared; conclusion present. Developing: advantages stated but limited comparison with culture; no real evaluation. Emerging: describes monoclonal antibodies without comparing to culture or evaluating.

practice_questions.text: Describe the steps involved in producing monoclonal antibodies for use in a diagnostic test.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: antigen injected into an animal to stimulate immune response; antibody-producing cells taken from the animal; cells producing the correct antibody are selected; these cells are cultured to produce large quantities of identical antibodies all recognising the same antigen. Steps in order, all four present. Secure: three steps correct. Developing: two steps described; sequence not fully correct. Emerging: general reference to antibodies being produced without describing the process.

practice_questions.text: A parent is deciding whether to vaccinate their child against a common disease. The child is healthy and many children in the class are already vaccinated. Using ideas about risk, benefit and decision-making, discuss the factors the parent should consider.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: benefits of vaccination (protection for child, memory cells, rapid response if infected); risks of vaccine (minor side effects, rare adverse reactions); herd immunity argument (most classmates immune, so risk to unvaccinated child is currently lower); but if too many parents reason this way herd immunity breaks down and disease resurges; individual right to decide vs societal responsibility; role of evidence and expert guidance; balanced conclusion with reference to weighing probability of harm (disease) versus probability and severity of vaccine side effects. Secure: benefits and risks addressed; herd immunity logic included; some weighing and conclusion. Developing: benefits and risks listed without weighing; herd immunity mentioned but not developed. Emerging: one-sided answer focusing only on vaccine risks or only on benefits.

practice_questions.text: State two differences between the primary and secondary immune responses.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: primary is slower / takes several days to produce significant antibody levels; secondary is faster / antibodies produced almost immediately due to memory cells. Two clear differences stated. Secure: one difference fully explained and one partially. Developing: one difference correctly stated. Emerging: vague reference to body recognising pathogen again without specifying what differs.

glossary_terms.definition: A preparation containing a safe form of a pathogen (dead, weakened, or parts of it) that is introduced into the body to stimulate an immune response without causing disease.
Proteins produced by lymphocytes that are specific to a particular antigen on a pathogen. They bind to the antigen to disable or tag the pathogen for destruction.
Molecules (usually proteins) on the surface of a pathogen that are recognised as foreign by the immune system and trigger an immune response.
Long-lived lymphocytes that remain in the body after an infection or vaccination and enable a rapid immune response if the same pathogen is encountered again.

The indirect protection that occurs when a sufficiently large proportion of a population has become immune to an infection, so reducing the spread of the pathogen and protecting those who cannot be vaccinated.
Antibodies produced in the laboratory from cloned immune cells, all of which recognise the same specific antigen. Used in diagnostic tests and medical treatments.

lessons.title: Lifestyle, Genes and Non-Communicable Disease
lessons.description: Correlation, cause and the everyday choices linked to long-term health.
lessons.content_html:
What Makes a Disease Non-Communicable?

Not all diseases spread from person to person. Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) are conditions linked to how we live, the genes we inherit, and the environment around us. They include cardiovascular diseases, type 2 diabetes, many cancers, and obesity-related conditions. Because NCDs develop slowly and are often preventable, understanding their causes is one of the most powerful tools in public health.

Scientists and doctors identify risk factors — variables that increase the probability of a disease developing. Identifying risk factors guides both individual choices and government health policy. Crucially, a risk factor is not the same as a cause: this distinction is at the heart of how we reason about evidence in science.

Key Fact

Non-communicable diseases cannot be transmitted between people. They are associated with risk factors — genetic, lifestyle or environmental — that raise the probability of disease. Having a risk factor does not guarantee a person will develop the disease.

Correlation vs Causation — The Critical Distinction

One of the most important ideas in science is the difference between correlation and causation. When two things tend to change together — for example, people who smoke more tend to have higher rates of lung cancer — we say there is a correlation. But correlation alone does not tell us that one variable is causing the other.

A confounding variable is a hidden factor that might explain a correlation without there being a direct causal link. For example, people who sleep very little also tend to drink more caffeine, exercise less, and have higher stress levels — any of these could be the true driver of a health outcome. Good epidemiological research tries to control for confounding variables by studying very large populations and using statistical techniques to isolate individual factors.

Moving from correlation to causation requires multiple lines of evidence. Scientists look for: (1) a plausible biological mechanism — can we explain why the factor might cause the disease at the cellular or physiological level? (2) a dose-response relationship — does more of the risk factor lead to greater disease risk? (3) consistency across studies — do researchers in different countries with different populations reach the same conclusion? (4) temporality — does exposure to the factor come before the disease develops?

Peer review is essential here. Results from a single study — even a large one — are not treated as definitive until they have been scrutinised by independent scientists and replicated. This is why scientific consensus on lifestyle and health has built up gradually over decades, not from a single dramatic finding.

Major Risk Factors for Non-Communicable Diseases

Research has identified a range of lifestyle, genetic and environmental factors associated with increased risk of NCDs. These include diet, physical activity, alcohol consumption, smoking, and inherited genetic variants.

Diet and obesity: A diet consistently high in saturated fats and added sugars is associated with raised blood cholesterol, fatty deposits in arteries, and increased risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. Carrying excess body fat — particularly around the abdomen — is correlated with insulin resistance, hypertension, and cardiovascular risk. BMI is commonly used as a screening tool, though it does not distinguish between muscle and fat mass.

Physical inactivity: Regular physical activity is associated with lower blood pressure, improved blood sugar regulation, and a reduced risk of both cardiovascular disease and certain cancers. Inactivity is itself treated as a risk factor, not just the absence of benefit.

Smoking: Tobacco smoke contains hundreds of harmful chemicals. Long-term smoking is strongly and causally linked (multiple mechanisms established) to lung cancer, coronary heart disease, and stroke. It also raises the risk of several other cancers. Smoking during pregnancy is associated with lower birth weight in babies.

Alcohol: Excessive alcohol consumption over time is associated with liver disease, certain cancers, hypertension, and cardiovascular disease. There is a dose-response relationship — risk generally rises with increasing consumption. Occasional, moderate alcohol intake is harder to categorise from the evidence; confounding variables make this area complex.

Genetic Risk Factors

Some people inherit gene variants that raise their susceptibility to certain NCDs, regardless of lifestyle. For example, some individuals inherit a tendency to produce high levels of LDL cholesterol (LDL cholesterol), which increases cardiovascular risk even in people who eat a healthy diet. Similarly, certain gene variants increase the lifetime risk of developing type 2 diabetes.

Genetic risk factors interact with lifestyle factors — someone with a genetic predisposition to heart disease who also smokes and is physically inactive faces a compounded risk. This interaction makes it misleading to separate “genes” from “lifestyle” as if they operate independently. Understanding your genetic risk can motivate earlier lifestyle changes and more frequent health screening.

Key Fact

Genetic risk factors (inherited gene variants) and lifestyle risk factors (diet, exercise, smoking) interact. A person with a genetic predisposition to high LDL cholesterol faces even greater cardiovascular risk if their lifestyle also includes smoking or physical inactivity.

Cardiovascular Disease and Type 2 Diabetes

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) develops when fatty deposits accumulate inside artery walls — a process called atherosclerosis. These deposits narrow the artery, reducing blood flow and raising blood pressure. If a coronary artery becomes severely blocked, the heart muscle is starved of oxygen, leading to a heart attack. If a cerebral artery is blocked or bursts, the result is a stroke.

Type 2 diabetes involves the body’s cells becoming resistant to insulin. Blood glucose levels remain elevated after eating, putting stress on blood vessels and organs over time. It is strongly associated with obesity, physical inactivity and a diet high in refined sugars — but genetic factors also contribute. Unlike type 1 diabetes (an autoimmune condition), type 2 is often preventable through lifestyle changes, though it has a complex genetic component too.

Epidemiology is the scientific discipline that investigates the patterns of disease across populations. Epidemiologists use data from sources such as national health surveys, hospital records, and large cohort studies (which follow groups of people over many years) to identify which factors are associated with higher or lower rates of disease.

One challenge in epidemiology is the outlier. Within any large dataset, some individuals will have a very different outcome from the majority — a lifelong smoker who lives to a very old age, for example. Outliers do not disprove a risk factor; they remind us that risk is probabilistic, not deterministic. Scientists do not automatically remove outliers from data; they investigate whether there is a genuine reason (measurement error, a different genetic background) before deciding how to handle them.

Key Fact

Correlation means two variables tend to change together. Causation means one directly produces the other. To establish causation, scientists need a plausible biological mechanism, a dose-response relationship, consistency across studies, and evidence that exposure precedes disease.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on lifestyle and disease often use data — a graph, table or study description — and ask you to “evaluate the evidence.” This is an Ideas about Science question: you must comment on the quality of the evidence (sample size, confounding variables, correlation vs causation) not just describe the data. Avoid writing “the data proves X” — instead write “the data suggests X, but confounding variables such as Y cannot be ruled out.” For 6-mark evaluate questions, always weigh both sides before reaching a conclusion.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Non-communicable diseases are linked to genetic, lifestyle and environmental risk factors rather than pathogens — they cannot be passed between people.
  • Correlation shows two variables change together; causation requires a biological mechanism, dose-response relationship and consistent replication before scientists accept it.
  • Major lifestyle risk factors for cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes include poor diet, physical inactivity, smoking and excessive alcohol — but genetic predisposition interacts with all of these.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a ‘risk factor’ for a non-communicable disease.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A factor that increases the probability (or chance/likelihood) of developing a disease [1]; it does not guarantee that the disease will occur [1].
Secure: A factor that makes it more likely that someone will develop a disease, but does not mean they definitely will.
Developing: Something that raises the chance of disease.
Emerging: A thing that causes disease.

practice_questions.text: A study followed 10,000 adults for 20 years. It found that those who exercised fewer than 3 hours per week had a higher rate of cardiovascular disease than those who exercised more. A journalist reported: ‘Lack of exercise proves to cause heart disease.’ Explain why this conclusion is not fully supported by the evidence.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies that the study shows a correlation, not causation [1]; explains that confounding variables (e.g. diet, smoking, genetic factors) may account for the difference [1]; notes that one study is insufficient — findings need to be replicated [1]; recognises a plausible mechanism would need to be established [1]; conclusion is clearly stated and evidence weighed [1].
Secure: States correlation vs causation [1]; identifies at least one confounding variable [1]; recognises replication is needed [1]; one further valid point.
Developing: Identifies correlation vs causation or one confounding variable, with limited further development.
Emerging: States the study is not proof, with no scientific reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain how both genetic and lifestyle risk factors can contribute to the development of type 2 diabetes.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Genetic factors: some individuals inherit gene variants that increase insulin resistance or reduce insulin production [1]; Lifestyle factors: diet high in refined sugars / physical inactivity / obesity associated with insulin resistance [1]; interaction: genetic predisposition is amplified by lifestyle factors, compounding risk [1]; conclusion that neither acts in isolation [1].
Secure: One genetic factor [1] and one lifestyle factor [1] described; some reference to interaction.
Developing: Names risk factors without explaining their mechanisms.
Emerging: Names diabetes without linking to causes.

practice_questions.text: A researcher wants to investigate whether high BMI is a risk factor for cardiovascular disease. Describe how she could design an epidemiological study to investigate this, including what data she would collect and how she would control for confounding variables.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Large cohort study with participants at different BMI levels [1]; collect cardiovascular disease rates over time [1]; control for confounding variables e.g. smoking status, diet, exercise, age [1]; large sample size to ensure statistical reliability [1].
Secure: Describes collecting BMI and CVD data [1]; identifies need to control confounders [1]; two further valid points.
Developing: Basic method described; limited discussion of controls.
Emerging: States she would collect health data, with no further detail.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether the evidence that smoking causes lung cancer is stronger than evidence that eating saturated fat causes cardiovascular disease. Use your knowledge of how scientific evidence is evaluated.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Smoking-lung cancer: biological mechanism well-established (carcinogens in smoke damage DNA in lung cells) [1]; dose-response relationship clear [1]; consistent across many studies and populations [1]; Saturated fat-CVD: plausible mechanism (raises LDL, promotes atherosclerosis) [1]; but confounding variables harder to control in dietary studies [1]; reasoned conclusion on relative strength of evidence [1].
Secure: At least two valid points on each side; conclusion present.
Developing: Valid points on one side only.
Emerging: States one causes disease without evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Give one reason why an outlier in a dataset showing the relationship between alcohol consumption and liver disease should not automatically be removed from the analysis.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Outliers are part of the real data; removing them without justification would bias the results / they may represent genuine variation in the population / their cause should be investigated first (accept any valid equivalent).

Confounding variables such as overall diet quality or exercise levels may explain the pattern
The correlation is negative rather than positive
The study was not peer reviewed

A _____ variable is a hidden factor that influences both an apparent cause and an apparent effect, creating a false impression of a direct link.

A factor that raises the probability of developing a disease

glossary_terms.definition: A disease that cannot be passed from one person to another, caused by genetic, lifestyle or environmental factors rather than pathogens.
A factor that increases the probability of developing a disease; it does not guarantee the disease will occur.
A statistical relationship between two variables, where changes in one tend to accompany changes in the other, without implying causation.
A direct relationship where one factor produces an observed effect, established through multiple lines of evidence including mechanism and dose-response.
A third variable that influences both the apparent cause and apparent effect, which can create a false impression of a direct link between two variables.
Body Mass Index — a measure calculated from height and weight used to assess whether body weight is in a healthy range, though it cannot distinguish muscle from fat.
A group of conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels, including coronary heart disease, heart attack and stroke, often linked to atherosclerosis.
A metabolic condition where the body's cells do not respond properly to insulin, leading to elevated blood glucose levels, associated with obesity and genetic factors.
A type of lipoprotein that carries cholesterol in the blood; high levels are associated with a greater risk of fatty deposits building up in arteries.
The branch of medicine that studies the distribution, patterns and determinants of health and disease in populations, often using large-scale data.

lessons.title: Treating Disease — Drugs and Trials
lessons.description: How new medicines are developed, tested and evaluated. Key concepts and applications explained.
lessons.content_html:
Why We Need New Medicines

Developing a new medicine is one of the longest and most expensive processes in science. From initial discovery to reaching patients, it can take more than a decade. Most candidate compounds fail somewhere along the way — they may prove toxic, ineffective, or only marginally better than existing treatments. Understanding the pipeline from laboratory to pharmacy shelf is important both scientifically and as a lesson in how evidence informs decisions.

Medicines work by interacting with specific biological targets — receptors, enzymes, or pathways — to alter the body’s response to disease. Before any new drug reaches a patient, it must pass through a series of testing stages designed to establish that it is safe and effective. These stages generate the evidence base that regulators and clinicians use to decide whether a drug should be approved.

Stage 1: Preclinical Testing

Preclinical testing is carried out in the laboratory before any human volunteers are involved. Candidate compounds are tested on cells grown in culture and on animal models. These tests look at whether the drug has any biological activity against the target, whether it is toxic to cells at the doses being considered, and how the body metabolises and eliminates it.

Preclinical testing narrows down a large number of candidates to a smaller set that appears promising enough to justify human trials. It does not guarantee safety in humans — human physiology differs from animal physiology in important ways — but it removes the most obviously dangerous or ineffective candidates before any person is put at risk.

Key Fact

Preclinical testing uses cells and animals to check a drug’s basic safety and biological activity before any human testing begins. It eliminates the most dangerous or ineffective candidates but cannot guarantee human safety.

Stage 2: Clinical Trials

Clinical trials test new drugs in human participants. They proceed in phases, each with a different goal. Early phases use small numbers of healthy volunteers to establish that the drug is safe and to find an effective dose range. Later phases involve larger groups of patients with the target disease to test whether the drug actually works.

Phase 1 — a small number of healthy volunteers (typically a few dozen). The aim is to test safety, identify side effects, and determine how the drug behaves in the human body (pharmacokinetics). Doses start very low and are gradually increased.

Phase 2 — a larger group of patients with the target condition (typically hundreds). The aim is to gain initial evidence of effectiveness and to refine the dosing. Researchers also continue monitoring safety.

Phase 3 — a large-scale trial involving many hundreds or thousands of patients, often across multiple hospitals and countries. The drug is compared against the current best treatment (or a placebo, if no treatment exists). This phase provides the main evidence used by regulators to decide on approval.

Post-approval surveillance (Phase 4) — once a drug is approved and in use, monitoring continues in the general population. This can detect rare side effects that were too uncommon to appear in clinical trials.

Placebo Controls and Blind Trials

A placebo is an inactive substance that looks and feels identical to the real drug. Using a placebo as a control is essential because patients who believe they are receiving treatment often report improvements in symptoms — this is the placebo effect. Without a placebo control, it is impossible to know whether any improvement is due to the drug itself or to the psychological expectation of getting better.

To prevent bias from influencing results, trials use blinding. In a double-blind trial, neither the participants nor the researchers who are administering the treatment know who is in which group. The allocation is randomised and the code is only broken after all data have been collected. This prevents both patients and doctors from unconsciously behaving differently based on their knowledge of who received the drug.

Key Fact

A placebo control allows the true drug effect to be separated from the placebo effect. In a double-blind trial, neither the patient nor the administering researcher knows who receives the drug — this removes bias from both reporting and administration. Randomisation ensures the groups are comparable.

Antibiotics and the Problem of Resistance

Antibiotics are medicines that kill or slow the growth of bacteria. They work by targeting structures or processes that bacteria have but human cells lack — for example, bacterial cell walls or particular enzymes. This selectivity is what makes them useful: they harm the pathogen without (ideally) harming the patient.

However, bacteria reproduce rapidly and can evolve resistance. Antibiotic resistance arises when random mutations give some bacterial cells a survival advantage against the drug. These bacteria survive, reproduce, and pass on the resistance. Over time, if antibiotics are overused or misused — for example, taken for viral infections, or not completed as prescribed — resistant strains become dominant in a population.

MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is a well-known example of a drug-resistant bacterium. It is resistant to many commonly used antibiotics, making infections difficult to treat. MRSA spreads most readily in environments where many people are in close contact and where antibiotic use is high — hospitals are a particular concern.

Reducing antibiotic resistance requires coordinated action: doctors prescribing antibiotics only when appropriate, patients completing their courses, and researchers developing new classes of antibiotics. The pipeline for new antibiotics has slowed in recent decades because the development costs are high and the commercial returns are lower than for drugs used long-term. This creates a genuine public health challenge that involves both scientific and economic decision-making.

Peer Review and Evaluating Drug Evidence

When clinical trial results are published, they are subject to peer review. Reviewers who were not involved in the trial examine the methodology, statistical analysis, and conclusions. They may identify flaws, request additional data, or reject the paper if the evidence is insufficient. Peer review does not guarantee a paper is correct — errors can still slip through — but it provides an important quality filter.

Evaluating drug evidence also involves considering conflict of interest. Research funded by a pharmaceutical company that manufactures the drug being tested may be subject to reporting bias — the tendency for positive results to be published more readily than negative ones. Independent replication by separate research groups, and access to full trial data (not just selected results), strengthens the evidence base considerably.

Key Fact

Peer review subjects scientific findings to scrutiny by independent experts before publication. Conflict of interest — especially industry funding — can introduce bias. Independent replication and full data access are important safeguards.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions about clinical trials, make sure you know the specific function of each design feature: the placebo eliminates the placebo effect, randomisation makes the groups comparable, and double-blinding removes bias from both the patient and the researcher. Extended-response questions often ask you to “evaluate the design of a study” — identify what was done well, what is missing, and how it could be improved. Avoid vague statements; link each point to why it matters for the reliability of the results.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • New drugs pass through preclinical testing (cells and animals) and then phased clinical trials before approval — the process is designed to establish safety and effectiveness at each stage.
  • Double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trials are the gold standard for testing medicines because they minimise bias and allow the true drug effect to be measured.
  • Antibiotic resistance develops through natural selection when resistant mutations survive drug exposure — overuse and misuse accelerate this process, making it a major public health challenge.

practice_questions.text: Explain why preclinical testing cannot guarantee that a drug will be safe in humans.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Human physiology differs from animal physiology [1]; effects observed in animal models or cell cultures may not replicate in the human body [1].
Secure: States that animals and humans are different, so results may not apply to humans.
Developing: Says animals are not humans.
Emerging: Says testing is done on animals.

practice_questions.text: A new antibiotic is tested in a clinical trial. Half the patients receive the antibiotic; half receive a placebo. Neither the patients nor the doctors administering treatment know who is in which group. Explain what type of trial this is and why this design is important.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies double-blind trial [1]; explains that neither patient nor researcher knows who is in which group, preventing bias in symptom reporting and administration [1]; placebo controls for the placebo effect so any improvement in the antibiotic group can be attributed to the drug [1].
Secure: Names double-blind [1]; explains one source of bias it removes [1].
Developing: States neither group knows, without explaining why this matters.
Emerging: Describes the design without linking it to reliability.

practice_questions.text: Describe how antibiotic resistance develops in a bacterial population over time.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Random mutation gives some bacteria a survival advantage against the antibiotic [1]; these bacteria survive and reproduce, passing the resistance gene to offspring [1]; over time the resistant strain becomes dominant in the population [1].
Secure: Mutation leads to resistance [1]; resistant bacteria reproduce more [1].
Developing: States bacteria become resistant after exposure, without explaining the mechanism.
Emerging: Says bacteria get used to the antibiotic.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that results from a clinical trial funded by the company manufacturing the drug provide reliable evidence for its effectiveness.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States trials can still be rigorous regardless of funding [1]; identifies conflict of interest as a genuine concern (company may benefit financially from positive results) [1]; reporting bias — positive results more likely to be published than negative ones [1]; peer review provides some protection [1]; independent replication by separate groups strengthens confidence [1]; balanced conclusion weighing evidence quality against potential bias [1].
Secure: Identifies conflict of interest [1]; one further valid evaluative point [1]; limited conclusion.
Developing: States company funding may be biased without explaining mechanism.
Emerging: Simply agrees or disagrees without evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why antibiotics are not prescribed for viral infections such as influenza.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: Antibiotics kill or inhibit bacteria by targeting bacterial structures; they have no effect on viruses (accept: viruses lack the structures that antibiotics target).

practice_questions.text: A clinical trial for a new pain-relief drug has 40 participants in total. Suggest two ways in which the reliability of the trial could be improved.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two valid improvements: Increase the sample size (40 is very small) [1]; use a double-blind design if not already in place [1]; ensure randomisation of participants to drug/placebo groups [1]; extend the trial duration to detect long-term effects or delayed side effects [1]. (Accept any two.)

knowledge_checks.q: What is the main purpose of the placebo in a clinical trial?
options: To provide a second active treatment for comparison
To eliminate the placebo effect so the drug's true benefit can be measured
To reduce the cost of the trial
To test whether participants can detect the difference between treatments

Testing a drug on cells and animals before human trials

glossary_terms.definition: A protein on or in a cell that a drug binds to in order to produce its effect, such as an enzyme or ion channel.
Testing a drug on cells, tissues and living organisms before any clinical trials begin, to assess basic safety and biological activity.
A controlled study of a new drug or treatment in human volunteers, designed to assess safety, optimal dosage and effectiveness.
An inactive substance or treatment, identical in appearance to the drug being tested, given to a control group to separate the true drug effect from the placebo effect.
A clinical trial design in which neither the participants nor the researchers administering the trial know which participants are receiving the drug and which are receiving the placebo.
A type of medicine that kills or inhibits the growth of bacteria by targeting bacterial structures; not effective against viruses.
The ability of bacteria to survive exposure to an antibiotic that would previously have killed them, arising through natural selection acting on random mutations.
Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus — a bacterial strain resistant to many common antibiotics, posing serious risk especially in hospital settings.
The process by which scientific work is scrutinised by independent experts before publication, to check for errors, methodological weaknesses, and unsupported conclusions.
